interviewQuestions.question: What are the most common non-technical mistakes that cause otherwise strong candidates to fail a coding round?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The ones I watch for in myself are almost all behavioral rather than algorithmic: coding before stating an approach out loud, acknowledging an interviewer's pushback verbally but not actually changing course, writing code with single-letter names and no structure under time pressure, losing track of the clock across a multi-problem round, and over-engineering a fifteen-line problem with unnecessary abstraction.

What makes these dangerous is that they're orthogonal to knowing the right technique — a candidate can know exactly the correct algorithm and still fail by triggering two or three of these in the same round, because interview scoring is usually multi-axis: correctness, communication, complexity, and code quality are each graded, and a strong score on one doesn't offset a weak score on another.

For example, someone who silently jumps into a correct sliding-window solution without saying so first has already lost communication credit before a single bug appears. My personal pre-round check is short: state the approach before typing, actually act on any pushback rather than just acknowledging it, keep variable names readable, and check in on time explicitly partway through.

**Testing:** whether you're aware that these habits, not raw algorithm knowledge, are what most often separates a pass from a fail.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The recurring mistakes

interviewQuestions.question: Why might a candidate over-engineer a simple coding problem, and why is that a mistake?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It usually comes from a good instinct applied at the wrong scale — the same instinct that serves you well designing a real production system (interfaces, dependency injection, config objects) gets reflexively applied to a problem that's genuinely solved by a fifteen-line loop, because the candidate associates more structure with looking more senior.

It's a mistake for two concrete reasons. First, it burns limited time on unneeded scaffolding instead of correctness and testing — building a `Strategy` interface and three helper classes eats minutes that should go to tracing edge cases. Second, and more subtly, it often signals the opposite of the seniority it's meant to project: real senior judgment is matching solution complexity to problem complexity, and defaulting to maximum structure regardless of scale reads as not having that calibration yet.

The practical fix is a one-line self-check before adding any abstraction: does the problem as literally stated need this, or am I adding it out of habit? A direct, well-named, fully-tested fifteen-line function usually scores higher than a scattered multi-file version of the same logic, and it leaves far more time to actually finish and verify the solution.

**Testing:** whether you can calibrate solution complexity to the actual problem instead of defaulting to maximum structure.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Over-engineering a simple problem

interviewQuestions.question: How do you make sure you don't run out of time on a multi-problem round?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I treat the round's time budget as explicit, not something to discover by running out of it. A 45-minute round with two problems usually implies roughly 15-20 minutes for the first so there's real time left for a second, likely harder one — spending 35 minutes perfecting the first problem's edge cases is a classic way to fail the round by never attempting the second at all, even though the first solution was excellent.

Concretely, I check in on time out loud at natural checkpoints: right after I've stated my approach ("this should take about 15 minutes to implement and test"), and again once I have a working first version ("I'm about 20 minutes in with something working — let me do a quick edge-case pass and then we can move to the next one"). Narrating this does two things: it keeps me honest about the clock instead of losing track while heads-down, and it shows the interviewer time-awareness they'd otherwise have to manage for me by interrupting.

If I do end up short on time for the second problem, I'd rather state a correct-but-unoptimized approach clearly than rush a half-finished optimal one, since a stated, reasoned approach still earns real credit even without full implementation.

**Testing:** whether you manage the round's time budget proactively instead of being surprised by the clock.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Time management across problems

interviewQuestions.question: You've noticed these pitfalls rarely happen in isolation — why do they tend to compound, and how would you break the chain as a candidate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
In debriefs, interviewers rarely describe a single isolated slip — they more often describe a pattern: the candidate coded silently, then also lost track of time, then also didn't react when nudged. Any one of these alone is usually recoverable and doesn't sink a round on its own; two or three together read as a genuine pattern rather than a one-off, which is what actually drives a no-hire decision on an otherwise-correct solution.

The mechanism is that one slip changes your state in a way that makes the next slip more likely. Getting briefly stuck and freezing tends to make you skip stating your next approach when you resume, because narration has already lapsed — and having stopped narrating makes it easier to miss or under-react to an interviewer's hint, since you're no longer in a mode of actively checking in with them. Each step is a small, individually forgivable lapse, but the chain reads very differently from any single link.

As a candidate, the way I break this is by treating the *first* slip as the actual event to catch, rather than waiting to notice the pattern after several have already happened — the moment I notice I've gone quiet, I explicitly resume narrating rather than waiting for a natural stopping point, precisely because that resumption is what prevents the next link in the chain.

**Testing:** whether you understand the pitfalls as a compounding system rather than a checklist of independent, equally-weighted mistakes.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why pitfalls compound
